questions.stem: A hospitalized client with type 1 diabetes is found unresponsive and sweaty at 0300. The capillary glucose is 38 mg/dL, and the client has a patent IV line. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Squeeze a tube of glucose gel inside the client's cheek
Give 50% dextrose IV per protocol
Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes to confirm it
Call the provider and wait for a new prescription

rationale.correct: Severe hypoglycemia: IV dextrose when there is IV access, or glucagon (IM, subcutaneous or intranasal) when there is not.

perOption.a: An unresponsive client cannot swallow safely.
perOption.b: IV dextrose rapidly corrects severe hypoglycemia when there is IV access.
perOption.c: Waiting delays treatment of a dangerous low.
perOption.d: Hypoglycemia protocols allow the nurse to treat immediately.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Treat severe hypoglycemia in a client who can't swallow.

questions.stem: A client with diabetes is shaky and sweaty with a glucose of 62 mg/dL. The client is alert and able to swallow. Which snack should the nurse give first?

options.text: 4 oz (120 mL) of fruit juice
A cheese stick and crackers
A chocolate candy bar
The full lunch tray now

rationale.correct: The 15-15 rule: give 15 g of fast carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat if still below 70 mg/dL.

perOption.a: This provides about 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate.
perOption.b: Protein and fat raise glucose slowly.
perOption.c: The fat in chocolate slows absorption.
perOption.d: Fast carbohydrate comes first; a meal follows once the glucose recovers.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Treat mild hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes who started metoprolol last month says, "I had a sugar of 48 yesterday and didn't feel anything until I got confused." Which explanation should the nurse give?

options.text: Metoprolol blocks warning signs such as a racing heart and shakiness
Metoprolol raises blood glucose, so lows are less likely to happen
Metoprolol causes heavy sweating that hides the usual symptoms
Metoprolol makes people sleep more deeply, so they miss the low readings

rationale.correct: Beta-blockers can mask the adrenergic symptoms of hypoglycemia; clients should check their glucose more often.

perOption.a: Beta-blockers blunt the adrenergic response that causes palpitations and tremor; sweating may still occur.
perOption.b: Beta-blockers can mask and prolong hypoglycemia rather than raise glucose.
perOption.c: Sweating is not increased.
perOption.d: This is not the mechanism.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize medications that mask hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes is admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis. The glucose is 540 mg/dL, the potassium is 4.8 mEq/L, and the heart rate is 128/min. Which prescription should the nurse start first?

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride bolus
Subcutaneous insulin glargine 20 units
IV sodium bicarbonate infusion
A carbohydrate-controlled diet

rationale.correct: DKA treatment order: fluids, check potassium, IV insulin, then add dextrose once the glucose falls to about 200 to 250 mg/dL.

perOption.a: Severe dehydration is the immediate threat; fluids restore perfusion and lower the glucose.
perOption.b: DKA needs IV regular insulin, started after fluids and a potassium check.
perOption.c: Bicarbonate is rarely used, and only for very severe acidosis.
perOption.d: The client is not ready to eat.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Begin DKA treatment in the correct order.

questions.stem: A client recovering from DKA has been on an IV insulin infusion for 20 hours. The anion gap has closed, the bicarbonate is 21 mEq/L, and the client is eating breakfast. The provider prescribes subcutaneous insulin glargine and stopping the infusion. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stop the insulin infusion now, then give the glargine at bedtime
Give the glargine and keep the infusion running 1 to 2 hours
Keep the infusion until the glucose falls below 100 mg/dL
Stop the infusion and give glargine once the glucose rises

rationale.correct: When moving from IV to subcutaneous insulin after DKA, give the basal dose and overlap the infusion by 1 to 2 hours.

perOption.a: A gap with no insulin lets ketones return quickly.
perOption.b: Overlapping prevents a gap in insulin, because IV insulin acts for only minutes.
perOption.c: The infusion is not continued to reach that target.
perOption.d: Waiting for the glucose to rise invites rebound ketoacidosis.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Transition insulin safely after DKA.

questions.stem: Before starting an insulin infusion for DKA, the nurse sees the potassium is 3.0 mEq/L. The glucose is 610 mg/dL and the pH is 7.12. Why is the potassium result important?

options.text: Insulin will push the potassium up to a dangerously high level quickly
Insulin drives potassium into cells, so it is corrected first
The potassium does not matter once fluids are running
A low potassium shows that the DKA is already resolving

rationale.correct: In DKA, total body potassium is low even when the blood level looks normal. Hold insulin if the potassium is below 3.3 mEq/L and replace it first.

perOption.a: Insulin lowers potassium.
perOption.b: Starting insulin with a potassium below 3.3 mEq/L can cause life-threatening hypokalemia.
perOption.c: Potassium shifts are a major risk.
perOption.d: This is not a marker of resolution.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Check potassium before starting insulin in DKA.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the laboratory results and the nurse's note for a newly admitted client. Complete the sentence.

content.template: The client's findings are most consistent with {{b1}}, and the nurse's first priority is {{b2}}.

options.text: diabetic ketoacidosis
hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
severe hypoglycemia
IV fluid replacement
diabetes diet teaching
an IV glucagon dose

rationale.correct: DKA: glucose above 250 mg/dL, pH below 7.30, bicarbonate below 18 mEq/L and ketones; start with fluids.

perOption.b1:a: High glucose, low pH and bicarbonate, and ketones show DKA.
perOption.b1:b: HHS has little or no ketosis and usually a pH above 7.3.
perOption.b2:a: Dehydration is the most immediate threat.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize DKA and its first treatment.

exhibits.title: Nurse's note
exhibits.body: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes has had vomiting and abdominal pain for 1 day. Deep, rapid breathing; fruity breath odor. Dry mucous membranes. Heart rate 124/min.

questions.stem: The emergency department nurse is caring for two clients with severe hyperglycemia, one with DKA and one with HHS. For each finding, choose the condition it is more typical of.

rows.text: Positive serum ketones with a pH of 7.15
Glucose of 940 mg/dL with serum osmolality of 350 mOsm/kg
Older adult with type 2 diabetes and gradual onset over days

rationale.correct: DKA = ketoacidosis, often type 1, rapid onset; HHS = extreme hyperglycemia and dehydration without significant ketosis, often type 2.

perOption.r1:c1: Ketoacidosis is the hallmark of DKA.
perOption.r1:c2: HHS has minimal ketones and a near-normal pH.
perOption.r2:c1: DKA glucose is usually lower, often 250 to 600 mg/dL.
perOption.r2:c2: Extreme hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality define HHS.
perOption.r3:c1: Deep, rapid breathing compensates for metabolic acidosis.
perOption.r3:c2: HHS has little acidosis to compensate for.
perOption.r4:c1: DKA usually develops over hours, often in type 1 diabetes.
perOption.r4:c2: HHS develops slowly in older adults with type 2 diabetes.
perOption.r5:c1: Dehydration occurs in DKA but is usually more profound in HHS.
perOption.r5:c2: HHS causes extreme dehydration and neurological changes.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish DKA from HHS.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old client with type 2 diabetes is brought in from a nursing home with confusion, a glucose of 880 mg/dL, no ketones and a blood pressure of 88/54. What is the priority intervention?

options.text: Rapid IV fluid replacement
An IV sodium bicarbonate infusion
A higher dose of the client's oral glipizide
Fluid restriction to protect the heart

rationale.correct: Fluid replacement is the cornerstone of HHS treatment, followed by insulin and electrolyte replacement.

perOption.a: Severe dehydration is the main problem in HHS.
perOption.b: HHS does not involve significant acidosis.
perOption.c: Oral agents are too slow and not appropriate in the acute phase.
perOption.d: This would worsen the dehydration.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize care in HHS.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes has influenza with nausea and is eating very little. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching about sick-day management?

options.text: "I'll check my blood sugar every 3 to 4 hours while I'm sick."
"I'll skip my long-acting insulin since I'm not eating."
"I'll test for ketones if my sugar is over 240."
"I'll sip sugar-free fluids often to stay hydrated."

rationale.correct: Sick-day rules: keep taking insulin, monitor glucose and ketones, drink fluids, and call the provider if vomiting continues or ketones are moderate to high.

perOption.a: Frequent checks are recommended.
perOption.b: Illness raises glucose; basal insulin must continue to prevent DKA.
perOption.c: Ketone testing is recommended.
perOption.d: Fluids prevent dehydration.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach sick-day rules for diabetes.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old client with type 2 diabetes cannot feel a monofilament on either foot. Which foot-care instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Look at your feet every day, using a mirror if needed
Dry your feet well, especially between the toes
Wear shoes or slippers at all times, even indoors
Have toenails trimmed straight across or by a podiatrist
Soak your feet in hot water every evening
Warm cold feet with a heating pad at night

rationale.correct: Neuropathy hides injuries; daily inspection and protection prevent ulcers and amputations.

perOption.a: Daily checks catch injuries early.
perOption.b: Moisture between the toes promotes infection.
perOption.c: This protects numb feet from injury.
perOption.d: This prevents ingrown nails and cuts.
perOption.e: Soaking dries the skin, and reduced sensation risks burns.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach foot care for diabetic neuropathy.

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes and reduced kidney function who takes metformin 1,000 mg twice a day calls the clinic. Which report should the nurse address first?

options.text: Mild diarrhea that started in the first week of taking it
Muscle aches, fast breathing and unusual sleepiness
A metallic taste in the mouth after taking the dose
A question about whether to take it with meals

rationale.correct: Metformin rarely causes lactic acidosis; the risk is higher with kidney impairment, contrast dye and heavy alcohol use.

perOption.a: GI upset is common early and usually improves.
perOption.b: These may be signs of lactic acidosis, a rare but serious adverse effect.
perOption.c: This is a minor side effect.
perOption.d: This is a teaching question; taking it with meals reduces GI upset.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize signs of metformin-associated lactic acidosis.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old client who lives alone and often skips lunch is starting glipizide 5 mg before breakfast. The client's A1C is 8.4% and creatinine is normal. Which adverse effect is most important for the nurse to teach about?

options.text: Hypoglycemia
Weight loss
Lactic acidosis
Genital yeast infections

rationale.correct: Sulfonylureas: take before breakfast, do not skip meals, and recognize and treat hypoglycemia; older adults are at higher risk.

perOption.a: Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin release and can cause hypoglycemia, especially if meals are skipped.
perOption.b: Sulfonylureas often cause weight gain.
perOption.c: This is associated with metformin.
perOption.d: These are associated with SGLT2 inhibitors.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach about sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client with type 2 diabetes and heart failure is starting empagliflozin in addition to metformin. Which instruction should the nurse include?

options.text: "Report genital itching or discharge, and drink enough fluids."
"This medicine often causes low blood sugar when taken with metformin."
"Take it on the days when your sugar reading is high."
"Limit your water so the medicine stays concentrated."

rationale.correct: SGLT2 inhibitors: genital infections, UTIs, dehydration and rare euglycemic DKA; they also benefit heart failure.

perOption.a: SGLT2 inhibitors put glucose in the urine, raising the risk of genital yeast infections and dehydration.
perOption.b: With metformin alone, SGLT2 inhibitors rarely cause hypoglycemia.
perOption.c: It is taken daily.
perOption.d: Hydration is important.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach about SGLT2 inhibitors.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old client with type 2 diabetes and a BMI of 36 asks about starting semaglutide after a friend lost weight on it. Which finding in the client's history would contraindicate it?

options.text: A sister treated for medullary thyroid carcinoma
An A1C of 8.6% on metformin alone
Blood pressure of 142/88 on lisinopril
A history of gallstones removed 10 years ago

rationale.correct: GLP-1 agonists: watch for pancreatitis and GI effects; they are contraindicated with a history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN 2.

perOption.a: GLP-1 receptor agonists are contraindicated with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN 2.
perOption.b: This is a reason to add a drug, not a contraindication.
perOption.c: Hypertension is not a contraindication.
perOption.d: A past cholecystectomy is not a contraindication.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify contraindications to GLP-1 receptor agonists.

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes asks what a hemoglobin A1C of 9.2% means. What should the nurse explain?

options.text: Glucose has been high on average for about 3 months
The client's glucose is dangerously low at this moment
The client's diabetes is well controlled
The client does not have diabetes after all

rationale.correct: A1C shows long-term glucose control; a target below 7% is common for adults.

perOption.a: The A1C reflects average glucose over about 3 months; most adults aim for below 7%.
perOption.b: A1C does not reflect a single day.
perOption.c: 9.2% is well above target.
perOption.d: 6.5% or higher is diagnostic of diabetes.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Interpret a hemoglobin A1C.

questions.stem: A client who takes NPH insulin at bedtime has fasting glucose readings of 220 to 250 mg/dL each morning. The provider asks the client to check at 0300 for 3 nights, and the readings are 52, 48 and 55 mg/dL. Which explanation is most likely?

options.text: The dawn phenomenon
The Somogyi effect
Increasing insulin resistance
Too little bedtime insulin

rationale.correct: Somogyi effect: low at 0300 and high in the morning, so reduce the evening insulin or add a snack. Dawn phenomenon: normal at 0300 and high in the morning, so adjust the timing or dose.

perOption.a: In the dawn phenomenon, the 0300 glucose is normal or high.
perOption.b: Nighttime hypoglycemia triggers counter-regulatory hormones that cause rebound morning hyperglycemia.
perOption.c: This does not explain the nighttime lows.
perOption.d: More insulin would worsen the nighttime lows.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Tell the Somogyi effect from the dawn phenomenon.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old with type 1 diabetes checks the glucose before soccer practice. It is 290 mg/dL with moderate urine ketones. What should the nurse tell the client?

options.text: "Go to practice, since exercise will bring your sugar down."
"Skip practice today and follow your plan for ketones."
"Eat a snack with carbohydrate before you start practice."
"Exercise isn't safe for people with type 1 diabetes."

rationale.correct: Avoid vigorous exercise when glucose is above about 250 mg/dL with ketones, and carry fast carbohydrate during exercise.

perOption.a: Exercise with ketosis can worsen hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis.
perOption.b: Exercise is postponed when ketones are present.
perOption.c: The glucose is already high.
perOption.d: Exercise is beneficial when glucose is safe.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach safe exercise for diabetes.

questions.stem: The clinic nurse is reviewing screening results for four adults without known diabetes. Which result confirms a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?

options.text: Fasting glucose of 132 mg/dL on two separate days
A random glucose of 160 mg/dL with no symptoms
A hemoglobin A1C of 6.0% on a single test
A fasting glucose of 105 mg/dL this morning

rationale.correct: Diagnostic criteria: fasting glucose 126 or higher, A1C 6.5% or higher, 2-hour OGTT 200 or higher, or random glucose 200 or higher with symptoms.

perOption.a: A fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher, confirmed by repeat testing, is diagnostic.
perOption.b: A random glucose must be 200 or higher with symptoms.
perOption.c: This is in the prediabetes range (5.7% to 6.4%).
perOption.d: This is prediabetes (100 to 125).

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply diabetes diagnostic criteria.

questions.stem: A client diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 3 years ago has never had an eye exam and says, "My vision is fine, so I don't need one." What should the nurse tell the client?

options.text: "You need an eye exam about every 5 years."
"A dilated eye exam every year finds damage early."
"You're right; you can wait until your vision changes."
"An eye exam is needed just at the time of diagnosis."

rationale.correct: Clients with diabetes need an annual dilated eye exam, along with yearly kidney screening and foot exams.

perOption.a: This is too long between exams.
perOption.b: Annual screening finds retinopathy before symptoms, when treatment can prevent vision loss.
perOption.c: Early retinopathy has no symptoms.
perOption.d: Screening continues for life.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach routine screening for diabetes complications.

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes took mealtime insulin and then missed lunch. Highlight the findings that suggest hypoglycemia.

rationale.correct: Hypoglycemia causes adrenergic signs (sweating, tremor, palpitations) and neuroglycopenic signs (confusion, slurred speech).

perOption.s2: Diaphoresis is an adrenergic sign of hypoglycemia.
perOption.s6: Confusion reflects a glucose shortage in the brain.
perOption.s10: Cool, clammy skin is typical of hypoglycemia.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the signs of hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes who uses insulin glargine at bedtime and lispro with meals is NPO after midnight for a cholecystectomy at 0900. What should the nurse do about the client's insulin?

options.text: Hold the insulin from midnight until the client is eating again
Ask about a lower glargine dose and check the glucose often
Give the usual breakfast lispro dose at 0700 as it is scheduled
Switch to an oral diabetes drug until after surgery

rationale.correct: Type 1 diabetes always needs basal insulin; adjust it while NPO and monitor glucose closely.

perOption.a: People with type 1 diabetes always need basal insulin to prevent DKA.
perOption.b: The basal dose is usually reduced, not stopped, while NPO, with frequent glucose checks.
perOption.c: Mealtime insulin without food causes hypoglycemia.
perOption.d: Oral drugs do not work in type 1 diabetes.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage insulin for a client with type 1 diabetes who is NPO.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with type 1 diabetes asks the nurse about drinking alcohol at a wedding this weekend. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding?

options.text: "I'll drink before I eat so the alcohol doesn't raise my sugar."
"I'll drink with food and check my sugar, including at bedtime."
"I'll take a few extra units of insulin to cover the drinks."
"Alcohol won't affect my sugar if I stick to beer."

rationale.correct: Alcohol can cause delayed hypoglycemia; drink in moderation with food and monitor glucose, including overnight.

perOption.a: Alcohol without food increases the risk of hypoglycemia.
perOption.b: Alcohol stops the liver releasing glucose, so delayed hypoglycemia can happen overnight.
perOption.c: This increases the risk of hypoglycemia.
perOption.d: Any alcohol can cause hypoglycemia.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach safe alcohol use with diabetes.

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes uses an insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio of 1 unit per 15 g and a correction factor of 1 unit for every 50 mg/dL above 150 mg/dL. Before a lunch containing 75 g of carbohydrate, the glucose is 250 mg/dL. The client's basal insulin was taken last night. How many units of rapid-acting insulin should the client take?

rationale.correct: Meal dose: 75 g ÷ 15 g = 5 units. Correction: (250 − 150) ÷ 50 = 2 units. Total: 5 + 2 = 7 units.
references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Calculate a mealtime insulin dose with a correction.
